features.headline: What Aaron Rodgers' benching means for Steelers, his future
features.desc: The Steelers are starting Mason Rudolph this week over Aaron Rodgers. Why make this change now — and will it help? And is this really it for Rodgers?
body: So many of the great quarterbacks in NFL history end their careers in dramatically disappointing defeats.

Though Peyton Manning won his second Super Bowl in his final NFL start, Tom Brady went out as the quarterback of an 8-9 Buccaneers team with a 31-14 loss to the Cowboys in the wild-card playoff round. Dan Marino lost 62-7 to the Jaguars.
Drew Brees couldn't move the ball in a 30-20 playoff loss to the Vikings. Brett Favre and Steve Young were knocked out of starts by injuries and never returned.
For Aaron Rodgers, one of the greatest players in the history of the sport, the end might have come in much more mundane fashion.
In Rodgers' 267th career start, the Steelers lost 19-16 to an Eagles team with little to play for on a day when most of the headlines were devoted to ejected Pittsburgh wideout DK Metcalf.

Two days later, the Steelers revealed in a late-night social media post that they were benching Rodgers for backup Mason Rudolph and deactivating the future Hall of Famer for Friday's game against the Broncos.
Even given the struggles the Steelers have faced on offense this season, this has to qualify as a stunning turn of events.
At 6-4, Pittsburgh is still in the thick of the playoff picture, with a 70.7% chance of advancing to the postseason, per ESPN's Football Power Index. The Steelers don't appear to be rebuilding.
They appear to be suggesting that they're better off with Rudolph in the lineup than Rodgers.
There are a few questions that stand out from the story, and I want to touch on them here. There's one that I keep coming back to as I try to understand what's happening in Pittsburgh.

features.headline: 2026-27 MLB free agency, trade grades: Offseason analysis
features.desc: We've got you covered with grades and analysis on every winter signing and big offseason trade.
body: The 2026-27 MLB offseason is officially here, and we have you covered with grades and analysis for every major signing and trade as this winter — which is expected to include a labor stoppage — unfolds.
Whether it's a franchise-changing free agent signing or an unexpected blockbuster trade, we'll weigh in with what it all means for next season and beyond.

ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle and David Schoenfield will evaluate each move as it happens, so follow along here, as this story will continue to be updated. Check back in for all the most recent analysis.
Skubal to NYM | Peralta to BAL Sato to CHC | Gray to MIN | Bauers to BOS
This is the Jonathan India situation all over again, a two-year deal for an average (or worse) player based on... what? Prospect grade from six years ago?
Alec Bohm solves nothing for the Kansas City Royals and makes the bad trade of Maikel Garcia that much worse.
Bohm, assuming the plan is to replace Garcia at third base, is a godawful defender with an offensive profile that suggests 15-20 homers with the K as his home venue and a decent hit tool.
He has shown a propensity to punch above his weight in RBI slots, but he'll no longer be doing that while hitting behind Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper and Trea Turner.

I've got him projected for just 1.1 WAR despite those bat virtues because of the glove and negative value on the bases. I don't have him any better as an overall player than Nick Loftin, whom he supplants on the depth chart.
And as for moving Bohm to the outfield, if that's a thought, forget about it. He can't run and the Royals already have to deal with having Jac Caglianone playing out of position in right.

features.headline: MLB free agency tracker: 2026-27 offseason trades, moves
features.desc: We've got you covered on all the major MLB hot stove signings and trades.
body: The 2026-27 MLB hot stove was lit just days after the Milwaukee Brewers hoisted the franchise's first World Series championship trophy.
Which teams will go big to contend for the 2027 World Series title? And who will make the trades and signings that have everyone buzzing?
Below is a running list of notable transactions and updates from throughout the MLB offseason.
Third baseman Alec Bohm has agreed to a two-year deal with the Kansas City Royals, according to multiple reports.
Right-hander Freddy Peralta and the Baltimore Orioles are in agreement on a five-year, $125 million contract, sources tell ESPN.
Left-hander Kris Bubic and the Cleveland Guardians are in agreement on a one-year, $17.5 million contract, sources tell ESPN.
The Chicago Cubs have reached an agreement with Japanese Central League MVP Teruaki Sato on a six-year, $120 million contract, sources tell ESPN.
Star Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira and the Toronto Blue Jays are in agreement on a five-year, $80 million contract with an opt-out after the third season, sources told ESPN's Jeff Passan.
Catcher Tyler Stephenson and the Cincinnati Reds are in agreement on a three-year, $30 million contract with an opt-out after the second season, pending physical, sources tell ESPN.
The Chicago White Sox are in agreement with free agent outfielder Tyrone Taylor on a two-year, $17 million contract, sources confirmed to ESPN.
Infielder Ha-Seong Kim and the Detroit Tigers are in agreement on a one-year, $5 million contract, sources tell ESPN.

features.headline: From practice squad to prime time: A look at Milton's big chance on Thanksgiving
features.desc: Ex-Cowboys QB Milton is set to headline the Eagles' Thanksgiving game, can he make the most of it?
body: Patrick Mahomes. Josh Allen. Dak Prescott. Jared Goff. Caleb Williams. Joe Milton.

A Thanksgiving slate chock-full of household quarterback names has one notable exception, though there is some growing intrigue around the 6-foot-5, 246-pound 26-year-old who goes by the name of "Mr. Rocket."
He'll be making his third career start Thursday when the Philadelphia Eagles face the Dallas Cowboys (4:30 p.m. ET, Fox)

The popular nickname for him had been "Bazooka Joe" — a hat-tip to a right arm that might be as strong as any in the league — but he said last week he prefers Mr. Rocket because "bazookas only travel so far."
(It doesn't take more than a single interaction to realize confidence is not an issue for Milton.)
Rookie receiver Makai Lemon experienced that arm strength up close when Milton delivered a laser of an intermediate pass that was too hot to handle in Sunday's 19-16 win over the Pittsburgh Steelers.
DeVonta Smith had to rethink a previously held belief when he was unable to track down a Milton deep ball in that game.
"I felt I couldn't be overthrown," Smith said with a smile, "but he did it."

There were plays Sunday that spoke to his physical gifts, like on a third-and-long midway through the first quarter when he escaped pressure to his left and threw a dime to Darius Cooper along the sideline while on the run.

And he showed quality decision-making in spots, including on the game-deciding completion to Smith when he was tasked with calling one of two plays at the line of scrimmage based on the defensive look and correctly dialed up Smith's number.

features.headline: Solo Ball is ahead of schedule just in time for UConn
features.desc: Solo Ball was thought to be out for the season, but his injury recovery has progressed faster than expected.
body: BOSTON — It took four months for Solo Ball to figure out what exactly was wrong with his wrist — a process that included three MRIs, five X-rays and ended with a diagnosis of multiple torn ligaments and a recovery timeline of nine months.
It only took a couple of weeks for Ball to realize he was going to beat that timeline and return to the court for UConn this season.

Just six months after surgery and three months after his wrist cast was removed, Ball could make his 2026-27 debut for the Huskies as early as Wednesday night in Las Vegas against Duke. Coach Dan Hurley said earlier this week that Ball was a game-time decision.
"Early on, it was tough, but my teammates really helped me," Ball told ESPN after UConn's win over Michigan in Boston on Nov. 6.

"The coaching staff, everyone in the locker room, everyone that's been with us this whole time in the facility, they've just been helping me a lot. And the fans gave me a lot of confidence, too. It's a whole army. That's why I love UConn."

Ball's injury, ironically, happened in his best game of the 2025-26 season. He scored 26 points and made three 3-pointers in a Dec. 16 win over Butler but hurt his wrist while bracing for a fall. Prior to the injury, Ball averaged 15.4 points.
After missing a game with the injury, Ball averaged 11.7 points over his final 27 games of the campaign that ended in the national championship game.
But given that he earned All-Big East honors in 2024-25 after posting 14.4 points and leading the league by shooting 41.4% from 3, it was clear something was wrong with Ball.

features.headline: Inside LeBron's first game in Philly — more than two decades ago
features.desc: Nearly 25 years ago, LeBron won over Philly for the first time — inside one of the most iconic basketball arenas in the world.
body: Jeremy Treatman, a former high school assistant coach in the Philadelphia suburbs who was running a burgeoning company that staged big-time basketball events between the game's future stars, had just sent a message to Dru Joyce II, the new coach at St. Vincent-St. Mary High School in Akron, Ohio, the school famously led by one of the most highly touted prep prospects in the history of the sport.

Six months after a then-17-year-old LeBron James had appeared on the cover of Sports Illustrated accompanied by the headline, "The Chosen One," Treatman was pitching Joyce on choosing him to build James' hype even more.

How would you like to play at the Palestra in Philly? How would you like to play Madison Square Garden against Sebastian Telfair? How would you like to play at Ohio State? How would you like to play at University of Dayton? How would you like to play in the Dean Dome in North Carolina?
In Philly parlance, Treatman had him at, "Yo."

"He calls me the next day and he says, 'You can get us to play at the Palestra?!'" Treatman told ESPN. "I go, 'Absolutely! Of course.' He goes, 'I've always dreamed of playing in the Palestra. I've heard about this place my whole life.
"I was completely bluffing about the Palestra," Treatman said. "I hadn't talked to anybody."

NAMED BY UNIVERSITY of Pennsylvania professor William N. Bates, evoking the Greek term "palæstra" that describes an athletic competition surrounded by an audience, the Palestra was the home for Penn's basketball, volleyball and wrestling teams.
